article.overview: A sample transfer interface is the mechanism, container interface or handling procedure by which a sample moves from one containment element to another without losing its integrity. In sample-return missions this may mean moving material from a collection device into a storage container, from an ascent vehicle into an Earth-return capsule, or from a return capsule into a curation laboratory. The catalogue name describes a function rather than one standard device. Documented examples differ widely in scale, design and mission context, so this article treats the category as a set of interface types. It does not assign the category a single specification.
article.description: A transfer interface has to meet several requirements at once. It must keep the sample contained, avoid contamination from the spacecraft, the mechanism or the surrounding environment, preserve a documented chain of custody, and provide a mechanical path that can be carried out reliably, often by remote operation and sometimes in vacuum or low gravity. Transfers can be performed by robotic mechanisms, guided rails, rods, latches and closures. In early Apollo missions, astronauts loaded samples into a sealed return container by hand on the lunar surface. The interface is therefore part hardware and part procedure. Its design is defined by the points at which containers, vehicles and laboratory systems meet, and by the steps that must be verified before the sample is treated as secure.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The purpose of a sample transfer interface is to preserve the scientific value of a sample between collection and analysis. Its main functions are to protect sample composition, including volatile material; to limit contamination in both directions; to keep sample provenance and handling history traceable; and to allow samples to pass through each stage needed to return them to Earth. Applications include transfers between spacecraft in orbit, transfers between containers on a surface system or lander, and transfers into curation facilities where samples are opened, sub-sampled and catalogued. The interface does not make a scientific measurement itself. Its value lies in the integrity of the material it handles.
article.operating_principle: Transfer interfaces are generally built from three elements: a defined path, such as a guided channel, rail, arm trajectory or rod; a capture or latching feature that holds the container at its destination; and a sealing or closure step that maintains containment after the transfer. Documented systems combine these elements in different ways. The Apollo Lunar Sample Return Container was closed under vacuum so that its internal pressure was not higher than the ambient lunar pressure, and its protective covers were removed just before closure. For Chang'e-5 and Chang'e-6, Chinese National Space Administration (CNSA) reports describe a sample container moved from the ascender to the orbiter-returner after docking in lunar orbit. The detailed mechanical sequence for those transfers is described in technical literature that was not read for this article. For Hayabusa2, the curation facility used a transfer rod to move the sample catcher between clean chambers. The in-flight transfer from the sampler to the capsule container is not described in the JAXA pages read.
article.scientific_importance: A sample is only as useful as its documented history. Contamination, loss of volatile components, mixing of material from different sites, or undocumented handling can reduce or invalidate later analyses. Sample-return programmes therefore treat containers and transfer steps as part of the science rather than as logistics alone. The Apollo containers, the Chang'e-5 and Chang'e-6 in-orbit transfers, and the Hayabusa2 curation transfer each show a different point in the return chain where this interface matters. The interface itself is not a science instrument. Its importance is indirect, through the integrity of the samples it handles.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal mass, size or power figure for a sample transfer interface. Each example below is a specific historical or flown system. The sources read did not publish comparable mass, dimension or power values for all of them, so where no reliable value was found the article says so rather than estimating.

examples.name: Apollo Lunar Sample Return Container (ALSRC)
examples.type: Flown sealed return container (Apollo lunar surface missions)
examples.flight_status: Flown (Apollo missions; flown status taken from Smithsonian collection titles as summarised in search results)
examples.description: Smithsonian collection titles for Apollo ALSRC records include examples described as flown, including Apollo 14 and 17 and Apollo 12 items. Reported construction: an aluminium box with a triple seal and an aluminium mesh liner intended to absorb shock. Reported sealing: the box was closed under vacuum so that its internal pressure was no greater than ambient lunar pressure, and a Teflon film and cloth cover protected the seals during loading and was removed just before closure. Reported handling: after return, the containers were opened under controlled conditions at the Lunar Receiving Laboratory in Houston. These statements come from search-result summaries of Smithsonian collection records, which were not opened in full (see the limitations section). Dimensions, mass and internal volume are not verified in this article and should be taken from the primary collection or NASA curation records before reuse.
examples.construction_reported: Aluminium box with a triple seal and an aluminium mesh liner intended to absorb shock (reported in search-result summary; not verified from the record page).
examples.sealing_reported: Closed under vacuum so that internal pressure was no greater than ambient lunar pressure; Teflon film and cloth cover protected seals during loading and was removed just before closure (reported; not verified from the record page).
examples.qualification: Dimensions, mass and internal volume were not verified. The Smithsonian record should be checked before any figure is used.

examples.name: Chang'e-5 ascender-to-returner sample container transfer (2020)
examples.type: Flown in-orbit transfer between spacecraft in lunar orbit
examples.description: Type: flown in-orbit transfer between spacecraft. A CNSA-sourced English report, updated 8 December 2020, states that the ascender 'successfully rendezvoused and docked' with the orbiter-returner combination in lunar orbit, and that the samples collected on the Moon 'have been transferred from the ascender to the returner'. The report says the docking was 'earlier on Sunday' and gives no clock time for the docking or the transfer. The calendar date, 6 December 2020, is inferred from that wording and the page's update date. Container dimensions, transfer mechanism travel, locking method and sealing details are not verified in this article.
examples.qualification: Transfer timing given as 'Sunday' without a clock time; the calendar date is inferred. Mechanism dimensions and locking/sealing details not verified.

examples.name: Chang'e-6 ascender-to-returner sample container transfer (2024)
examples.type: Flown in-orbit transfer between spacecraft in lunar orbit
examples.description: Type: flown in-orbit transfer between spacecraft. A CNSA-sourced English report, updated 6 June 2024, states that the ascender 'successfully rendezvoused and docked' with the orbiter-returner in lunar orbit, and that the lunar samples were 'transferred safely from the ascender to the returner on Thursday'. The report states that the transfer was complete 'by 3:24 p.m.' without naming a time zone. The 6 June 2024 date is consistent with the page date. Container dimensions, mechanism details and sealing details are not verified in this article.
examples.qualification: Transfer completion given as 'by 3:24 p.m.' without a time zone. Mechanism details not verified in the fetched report.

examples.name: Hayabusa2 sample catcher and curation-side transfer (asteroid sample return; not a lunar example)
examples.type: Flown sample catcher and curation-side transfer
examples.description: Type: flown sample catcher and curation-side transfer. Hayabusa2 is included as a non-lunar sample-return example. JAXA's mission instrument page describes a sampler with a sampler horn, a projectile and a sample catcher, and states that a newly developed metal seal method is applied so that volatile gases such as rare gas can be returned. The page also describes the horn edge being folded inward so that gravel of 1 to 5 mm can be captured, and says that gravel would continue to be stored in the catcher if the spacecraft made an emergency stop while ascending. JAXA's Curation Center page describes the sample catcher sitting inside a sealed sample container delivered by the re-entry capsule. After the container's inner lid was opened in Chamber 3-1 on 14 December 2020, a transfer rod moved the catcher from Chamber 3-1 to Chamber 3-2. The catcher has three chambers, A, B and C, each able to store samples independently. The page reports a total sample mass of 5.424 plus or minus 0.217 g and a vacuum below 10 to the power of minus 5 Pa in Chambers 3-1 and 3-2. The vacuum value is a curation-laboratory condition, not a flight requirement. The JAXA pages read do not describe how the catcher is moved into the capsule container in flight.
examples.sample_mass_g_reported: 5.424 plus or minus 0.217 (total sample mass, curation; not hardware mass)
examples.curation_chamber_vacuum_pa_reported: Below 1e-5 Pa in Chambers 3-1 and 3-2 (curation laboratory condition, not a flight requirement)
examples.qualification: Flight transfer from sampler to capsule container not described in the JAXA pages read. Hardware dimensions and mass not verified.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: No comparable external dimensions are published for these transfer interfaces in the sources read. The Apollo container, the Chang'e in-orbit container and the Hayabusa2 catcher serve different purposes and should not be compared as if they were the same class of hardware. Any new interface would need its envelope set by the container it carries, the mechanism that moves it, and the mounting and clearance requirements of the vehicles on either side.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: No general mass value is given for a sample transfer interface. The Hayabusa2 sample total of 5.424 plus or minus 0.217 g is a sample mass, not a hardware mass, and should not be read as an interface mass. Hardware masses for the Apollo, Chang'e and Hayabusa2 transfer systems were not verified from primary sources in this article.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: No power requirement is verified for any of the examples. A transfer interface may be passive, manually operated or motor-driven depending on design, so power depends on the specific system and is not estimated here.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A transfer interface must operate in the environment of the vehicle or facility in which it sits. On the lunar surface and in lunar orbit this includes vacuum, large temperature swings, radiation, dust and the mechanical loads of launch, landing and ascent. The Apollo example shows the containment side of this requirement: sealing under vacuum and protection of seals from contamination during loading. The Hayabusa2 curation example shows a ground-side requirement: chamber vacuum below 10 to the power of minus 5 Pa during recovery and handling. Flight thermal, mechanical and contamination requirements for the Chang'e in-orbit transfer hardware and for the Hayabusa2 flight catcher are not publicly specified in the sources read. No universal environmental requirement for transfer interfaces is assumed.
article.limitations: The category name describes a function, so the article cannot provide one authoritative design. The available examples are heterogeneous. The Apollo container is a sealed box with documented handling; the Chang'e-5 and Chang'e-6 transfers are in-orbit spacecraft-to-spacecraft transfers reported at mission level; and the Hayabusa2 examples are asteroid sample hardware with a curation-side transfer. Many numerical values, including hardware dimensions, mass, transfer distances and seal or latch specifications, were not verified from primary technical sources. Several claims depend on search-result summaries rather than full-text documents. Chinese mission reports are relayed through CNSA-sourced English pages, and their wording should be treated as official statements rather than engineering data.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A sample transfer interface is a link in a sample-return chain rather than a payload that is delivered on its own. It is transported as part of a surface system, ascent vehicle, orbiter, return capsule or laboratory system. The steps below describe the general chain, with documented examples where the sources support them.
transportation_process: Collect material into a containment element, such as a scoop, catcher or sealed container, on the surface or from a sampling device.
Transfer the sample into a sealed storage container using a defined mechanical path, with the sample protected from contamination.
Seal the container and, where the design requires it, keep the sample under vacuum or inert conditions until its next transfer.
Stow the container in the ascent vehicle or lander payload and integrate it with the launch or landing system.
Transfer the container between spacecraft in lunar orbit, as reported for Chang'e-5 and Chang'e-6, before the Earth-return leg.
Return the container through atmospheric re-entry and recovery, and transfer it to a curation facility.
Open and sub-sample the container under controlled conditions, as in the Apollo Lunar Receiving Laboratory and the Hayabusa2 curation process.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: A sample transfer interface is not deployed in the sense used for instruments. Its operation depends on the mission. Apollo sample containers were loaded by astronauts on the lunar surface. Chang'e-5 and Chang'e-6 transfers were carried out between spacecraft in lunar orbit after docking. Hayabusa2 transfers in the curation facility used a rod to move the catcher between chambers. No specific robotic or crewed transfer method is recommended for a new interface in this article.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The Apollo ALSRC shows a crewed, sealed hand-loaded container on the Moon. The Chang'e-5 and Chang'e-6 reports show automated transfers between an ascender and an orbiter-returner after docking in lunar orbit. The Hayabusa2 curation process shows a rod-based transfer between sealed curation chambers after return from an asteroid.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with a named lander, ascender, orbiter, return capsule or curation system is claimed. A future transfer interface would need to be assessed against mass, envelope, mounting points, transfer loads, sealing and contamination requirements, power and data interfaces, and the verified interface documents of the vehicles on either side. None of these were verified for a specific spacecraft in this article.

article.historical_significance: The Apollo sealed return containers established a documented, sealed-return approach for lunar samples that relied on crew handling on the surface and controlled opening in a receiving laboratory. The Chang'e-5 and Chang'e-6 reports describe automated transfers of a sample container between spacecraft in lunar orbit, which is a different architecture from surface-to-Earth crewed return. The Hayabusa2 curation transfer shows how a sealed catcher is moved between chambers during analysis preparation. Together these examples show that the transfer step has been treated as a distinct engineering and curation problem in several sample-return programmes.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The term 'sample transfer interface' describes a class of hardware and procedures, not one standard design. The examples are not interchangeable. Values such as dimensions, mass, transfer distance, seal type and cycle counts must always be tied to a named system and its source. The Apollo ALSRC description depends on Smithsonian summaries that were not opened in full. The Chang'e-5 and Chang'e-6 descriptions depend on CNSA-sourced English reports that do not give mechanism details. The Hayabusa2 flight-transfer details are not fully described in the pages read. The generic environmental and transport discussion describes engineering considerations. It is not a certified design specification for a new payload.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url and source_page_url values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. Section-level image objects are repeated intentionally so each article section can render its own images without resolving IDs against the master gallery.

data_quality_notes: Apollo ALSRC construction, sealing, protective covers, shock liner and Lunar Receiving Laboratory opening statements come from search-result summaries of Smithsonian collection records. The record pages returned HTTP 403 and were not opened. Verify against the record pages before reuse.
No ALSRC dimensions, mass or internal volume were verified. These fields are not populated.

Chang'e-5 transfer date 6 December 2020 is inferred from the English report's 'Sunday' wording and its 8 December 2020 page date. The report gives no clock time. A secondary summary gives 06:12 Beijing Time on 6 December; it is not used because it was not confirmed in the report text.
Chang'e-6 'by 3:24 p.m.' is reported without a time zone. The report does not state the transfer mechanism's dimensions.

Chang'e-6 channel width of 200 to 300 mm, the approximately 36-minute transfer interval and the approximately 2 kg container capacity appeared only in search-result summaries and not in the fetched report text. They are not used as facts.
Chang'e-5 transfer travel of about 626 mm and three-segment guide rails appear only in search-result summaries of an MDPI Aerospace paper that returned HTTP 403. They are not used as facts.

The JAXA instrument page's wording on the number of sample catcher compartments ('increased by one to three compartments compared to two for the Hayabusa') is ambiguous and is not used. The page describes the capsule's return in future tense, so it is treated as pre-flight description.
A search-result summary reports a Hayabusa2 catcher-to-capsule transfer on 26 August 2019. It was not confirmed on the JAXA pages read and is not used.
Hayabusa2 chamber vacuum below 10 to the power of minus 5 Pa is a curation-laboratory value, not a flight requirement.

The Sawada et al. (2017) Hayabusa2 sampler paper was not read in full. Search results pointed to a mirror domain; the canonical DOI is used instead. Its storage-and-transfer mechanism description is not used as a fact.

NASA photo captions for ALSRC unloading at the Lunar Receiving Laboratory (NASA IDs S69-39996, S69-45002, S69-45507, S69-60294) and a NASA Photojournal training image (PIA24297) were identified only through third-party or search summaries. NASA image details page for S69-39996 returned no content. No direct image asset URL was verified, so none of these images is included.
